name: Men's makeup (contour, bronzer, highlight)

lead: Subtle contour, highlighter and bronzer make the jaw, cheekbones and nose look more defined, so the face looks sharper while the makeup is worn.

Contouring uses a shade one or two tones darker than the skin in hollows and along edges to create shadow, while highlighting uses lighter shades on prominent areas. It has roots in theatrical makeup, was popularised by a 2000 book, and went mainstream on social media in the 2010s.

paras: People apply a darker shade under the cheekbones and along the jawline, a lighter one on the high points, and blend until the edges disappear. Men usually keep it light so it reads as natural, and the effect is immediate.
Low risk. Makeup can irritate or break out sensitive skin, and heavy or poorly blended application is easy to spot.

social.title: Gen Z is making men's makeup go "mainstream." Gen X and the 1980s would like a word

chain: Darker shade in hollows, lighter on edges
Shadow and light change the face
angle.text: Darker shades in the hollows and lighter ones on prominent edges create shadow and light that make the jaw, cheekbones and nose look more defined. The effect is visible while worn and follows standard makeup practice.

lead: Men's makeup in this context refers to using contour (darker shades), highlighter (lighter shades) and bronzer to emphasize the jaw, cheekbones and nose. Contouring generally uses a shade one or two tones darker than the skin in hollows and along edges to create shadow, while highlighting uses lighter shades on prominent areas.[1]

Contouring has roots in theatrical makeup. Elizabethan stage actors used chalk and soot, and Max Factor Sr. presented a contouring tutorial in 1945. Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book popularized it, and social media made it mainstream in the 2010s.[1] Male cosmetics were a niche market until the late 1990s.[2]

paras: Contouring places warm or cool darker shades in the hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples to create a slimming, sculpted look. Highlighting uses lighter shades on the cheek apples, nose tip and T-zone, and strobing relies mainly on light shades.[1]

Wikipedia reports that male cosmetics are less widely accepted than female cosmetics, with men aged 18 to 34 more likely to use them, and that men cite covering blemishes, improving appearance and slowing visible aging as reasons.[2] Male beauty creators on YouTube produce tutorials and product reviews.[2]

Some looksmaxxing communities discuss subtle contour as a non-surgical way to enhance a defined jaw or cheekbone appearance, particularly for photos. Others regard makeup as outside the practice. The effect is optical and temporary.
No studies found. Published literature on male cosmetic contouring concerns surgical and device-based body contouring, which is a different subject.

lore.intro: Male contouring appears in looksmaxxing discussion as a cheap, reversible way to simulate stronger bone structure.

claims.claim: Contour and highlight can make the jaw and cheekbones look more defined.
Makeup carries stigma for men that limits its use.

timeline.event: Elizabethan stage actors use chalk and soot to define faces.[1]
Max Factor Sr. presents a contouring tutorial for different face shapes.[1]
Kevyn Aucoin's book Face Forward brings contouring to the public.[1]
Celebrities and brands make contouring and strobing mainstream.[1]
